docs.title: Dead Ridge, TN
docs.text:
Out here, in these mountains, the dead are the least complicated thing you'll face.

This is the session archive and campaign wiki for Dead Ridge, TN — a Walking Dead Universe Roleplaying Game campaign set in the Tennessee and Georgia mountains, five years after the outbreak. It's a record of who the survivors are, what they've done, what it cost, and the stretch of ridge that keeps testing them.

Read the Prologue first — that's what everyone at the table hears before anything else. Session zero has been played: the survivors have a haven, the mountains have their rules, and the pages below fill in as the campaign goes on.

docs.title: The Setup
docs.text:
What the mountains believe

Session zero settled it. The herds in this region climb — people have seen them in the trees. A walker was once seen to pause before attacking a child. Everyone navigates by a haunted school bus called the Old Yeller. And a man calling himself the Watchman is still broadcasting conspiracies from somewhere out past the dial — new ones each time, which means he's still alive.

  • System — The Walking Dead Universe Roleplaying Game (Free League)
  • When — 2030, five years after the outbreak
  • Where — the ridges above Soddy-Daisy, north of Chattanooga
  • Haven — the Hollow, a hunting cabin at the end of a washed-out logging road. Nine people, Capacity 1, Defense 2.
  • GM — Gary

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
1. Run session zero: the Unsetting Questions, haven selection, and character creation. Record the answers into world/world.md.
  2. Record and transcribe the session (see README.md), then drop the materials into sessions-raw/<DATE>/.
  3. Run the summarize latest session skill to generate the session page and the survivor, group, and location wiki entries, then build world data to rebuild this home page.
  4. publish site to push it live.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text: # Session Date 0 Nine in the Hollow 2026-08-30

docs.title: Prologue
docs.text:
The Walking Dead Universe Roleplaying Game — Tennessee/Georgia mountains, 2030.

It's 2030. Five years since it started, though nobody agrees on what "it started" really means.

Some people mark it from the first quarantine order. Some mark it from the last coherent news broadcast. Some mark it from the day their own street went quiet. Truth is, by the time anyone had a name for what was happening, it had already happened. Nobody saw it coming, because everybody was looking somewhere else — another war on another continent, another market crash, another feed of cat videos to scroll past at two in the morning. The world had gotten very good at watching a hundred disasters at once and taking none of them seriously. This one was different.

What should scare you more than the dead is how fast everything else fell. The nations that called themselves superpowers spent their last good months arguing about whose fault it was, instead of doing anything about it. Generals fought with politicians. Politicians fought with each other. By the time anyone agreed on what to do, there was no one left organized enough to do it. The scientists didn't do much better. All that knowledge, all those labs, all that certainty that a problem like this gets solved — and it turned out knowing what something is isn't the same as stopping it. The people who might have found an answer together spent too long fighting over who'd get the credit if they did, and who'd take the blame if they didn't. In the end, it didn't matter. There was no cure. There was no rescue. There was only what came next.

What came next was simple, and it hasn't gotten more complicated since. Every town, every hollow, every stretch of highway answers to whoever's strong enough to hold it. Groups write their own laws now, and enforce them however they see fit. Some of those laws keep people alive. Some of them get people killed just as fast as the dead do. You learn quickly which is which, or you don't survive long enough to learn anything at all.

People still talk about somewhere better — some say the government held on out west, that there's an America still standing behind walls and satellites and soldiers who never stopped taking orders. Nobody you've ever met has been there. Nobody you've ever met has met anyone who's been there. It's the kind of story people tell each other on bad nights, the same way they used to tell ghost stories — not because it's true, but because believing it costs nothing and might get you through till morning.

What's real is closer than that, and a lot less comforting. It's the sound a herd makes before you can see it. It's the quiet that comes right before a stranger's hand goes for a weapon instead of a handshake. Out here, in these mountains, the dead are the least complicated thing you'll face. The next encounter — whatever's on the other end of it — might be the last one you get.

Welcome to Tennessee. Welcome to Georgia. Welcome to what's left.

Where this leaves you

Five years in. No cure, no rescue, no authority left worth the name. What happens next in these mountains hasn't been decided yet — that's session zero. Bring a character who has already survived something.

docs.title: Nine in the Hollow
docs.text: Session zero · 2026-08-30

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Before a single die was rolled in anger, the table decided what everyone in these mountains believes: that the herds here climb, that a walker was once seen to pause before attacking a child, that the landmark you navigate by is a haunted school bus called the Old Yeller, and that a man calling himself the Watchman is still broadcasting conspiracies from somewhere out past the dial. Four survivors were built, four Anchors were chosen, and out of three possible homes the group took the cabin at the end of the washed-out logging road.

Nine people now live in a hunting cabin rated for far fewer.

docs.title: The Unsetting Questions
docs.text:
Each player rolled once, and the answers became canon:

  • The herd here climbs. People have seen them in trees, coming up the sides of the mountains the way bears do — over the hillside before you know they're there. This single answer quietly undid the group's entire reason for choosing high ground.
  • One paused before attacking a child. No explanation offered. Nobody liked it. It stayed.
  • The Old Yeller. A school bus whose driver had a heart attack behind the wheel and turned with a full load of kids aboard. Some say it's haunted. The name was arrived at by way of a groan-worthy pun that the table immediately and unanimously adopted. See the Old Yeller.
  • The Watchman. A conspiracy broadcaster named after the graphic novel he took too seriously — chemicals in the water, fluoride, all of it. The group specifically ruled that the broadcasts are not a loop: they change each time, so he's still alive. And one day he might go quiet. See the Watchman.

docs.title: Choosing a Home
docs.text:
Three havens were on the table: the Last Stop (an unfinished Buc-ee's), the Ark (a grounded houseboat in a cove), and the Hollow (a hunting cabin up a logging road).

The Buc-ee's was the one everybody wanted. It was also the one that would kill them — fifty pumps, a fifteen-foot fiberglass mascot visible for miles, more doors than anyone can watch, and a full propane cage out back. The group talked itself out of it inside a minute and then spent the rest of the session mourning it.

They took the Hollow, and placed it in a sector near Soddy-Daisy — river access, natural resources, not quite on top of Chattanooga.

Then came the twist that reframed the whole group: the Hollow is Johnathan Banks' family cabin, his father's or grandfather's. He was a rich, snarky punk with a place he barely used, and everyone else there is a straggler he took in against his better judgment.

docs.title: Four Survivors
docs.text:
• Johnathan Banks — Broker. Wall Street; ran insider trades for mobsters and hopes they're all dead. Carries no weapon, two sets of scales, and letters of introduction to three other havens. Drive: "I just gotta ring the bell."
  • Ashley "Ash" Fairfax — Nobody. College dropout and burnout who was delivering a pizza when the world ended, got caught in a herd, and ran into the woods. Issue: doesn't care if she lives. Drive: "Keeps going anyway."
  • Dr. Charles "Chuck" Greenbriar — Scientist. A biologist who really wanted to be a cryptozoologist and now believes the walkers prove he was right all along. Drive: "I'm not crazy."
  • Clara "CJ" James — Homemaker. A pilates-and-martial-arts soccer mom with no family left and a number she's trying to run up. Agility 5, the highest stat at the table. Issue: Bloodthirsty.

docs.title: Anchors
docs.text:
Five people were already living at the Hollow, and the survivors chose who they'd hold onto:

  • Banks took Sister Ruth Okafor — and the story behind it is the ugliest thing established all session. He met her at the retirement home, one of the havens he holds a letter for, and talked her into abandoning her patients: "Just read these people their last rites and then come help us."
  • Chuck took Dale Pruitt, the moonshiner who sheltered him before all this — "Dale sees things when he's at the bottom of a bottle. He feeds my delusions."
  • CJ took Birdie Coyle, the former park ranger, over a shared love of nature and growing things — the softest thing established about the group's most lethal member, and the only bond formed at the Hollow rather than carried into it.
  • Ash took nobody — she picked the Wallflower talent, making the whole group her anchor, on the stated logic that "I don't get as sad if one of them dies."

That leaves Tucker Vance and Marcus Webb unclaimed — the mechanic at a haven no vehicle can reach, and the fifteen-year-old who's desperate to be taken seriously.

docs.title: How They Know Each Other
docs.text:
• Banks and CJ were neighbors before — two wealthy households on the same street. He took her with him. It's the oldest bond in the group.
  • Chuck and Dale came in together, out of the woods, after being driven from Dale's cabin. Chuck had originally come to Chattanooga for the aquarium.
  • Ash is pure happenstance — she ran into the cabin the way she runs into everything. The GM named her the one everybody knows least.

docs.title: Memorable Moments
docs.text:
• King Buc-ee. Banks' player campaigning to run an unfinished travel plaza as a theocracy: "I'm gonna be King Buc-ee. And I'll spread the gospel of the beaver." Overruled on the grounds of near-certain death, and never let go of.
  • Zombie bears. The climbing-herd answer took roughly ten seconds to escalate from "they come up the hillsides like bears do" to a walker riding a bear.
  • Two sets of scales. Banks rolled the one gear item he didn't want — a set of merchant's scales — and then rolled it again. His justification: "In case one of them's off. I like to check my work." He ended the session with no weapon and two sets of scales.
  • Bigfoot got COVID. Chuck's origin theory for the outbreak, delivered straight-faced and immediately reinforced by the rest of the table, who realized the funnier move was to agree with him. "We're just all feeding your delusions." — "Because nobody's got the heart to tell me I'm crazy." — "Yeah. Because you have a gun and a hammer."
  • Walkers on walkers. The group's mental image of the retirement-home haven: survivors barricading themselves with mobility walkers, and the other kind of walker outside.
  • "I'm gonna do my best to make y'all wanna kill me but not kill me." Banks' player, stating his design goals for the campaign out loud.
  • The recording anxiety. Ten minutes in, the GM realized he hadn't written down a single Unsetting Answer: "I didn't write any of those down, so I'm hoping that thing is still recording." It was.

docs.title: Open Threads
docs.text:
• The herds climb. The Hollow's defense rating assumes the terrain protects it. The terrain does not protect it. Nobody has connected these two facts out loud yet.
  • Banks' three letters. The retirement home is confirmed as one. Banks names a second; the GM names the third. Whatever the third is, they haven't seen it coming.
  • Sister Ruth's patients. She left a building full of dying people because a stock trader asked her to. That bill has not been presented.
  • The Watchman may go silent. The group built in the possibility deliberately.
  • Something is still in there. One walker paused before a child. The Hollow has a fifteen-year-old in it.
  • Nobody anchored Tucker or Marcus. The man who fixes things and the kid who wants to matter are both unattached.
  • The root cellar is nearly bare and there are nine mouths. Winter is the clock.
  • PC-to-PC anchors were deferred to a later session.

docs.title: Next Session
docs.text: The GM has the first session sketched out. Weapon stats and remaining gear details still to be filled in on the sheets.

docs.title: The Scene
docs.text:
You could see it from the ridge, which was the first thing wrong with it. Fifty pumps under a canopy the size of a hangar, a storefront with its plate glass blown out into a glitter of safety cubes across the apron, and out front — still standing, still waving, five years into the end of the world — a fifteen-foot fiberglass beaver with a grin like a man who has never once been told no. The wind came across the lot and moved nothing except the weeds coming up through the asphalt. Banks stopped walking about forty yards out and just looked at it, and something happened to his face that none of the others had seen there before.

"There's jerky in there," he said. "There is dry storage. There is a gift shop the size of my first apartment building and it is full of things people used to drive four hours out of their way to buy." He turned around, walking backward, arms open, and for a moment he wasn't a man in a ruined suit at the end of a dead highway; he was working a room. "You put nine people in a cabin and you get nine people's problems in one room. You put nine people in there and you've got a town. I'm not asking to be in charge. I'm saying somebody has to be, and I'm saying I'd be good at it." Somewhere behind him the beaver kept waving. "I'd spread the gospel of the beaver," he said, and he almost had them.

CJ didn't answer. She had gone quiet the way she went quiet, and she was walking the front of the building, and she was counting. Storefront: four ways in, and that was just what she could see from here. Loading dock around the side. The fuel islands, open on every face, no wall between them and the treeline. Behind the building, a steel cage stacked to the top with propane cylinders that nobody had gotten around to dealing with because nobody had ever needed to. She came back and stood next to Banks and looked at it with him for a while, and when she finally spoke it wasn't unkind. "We'd die here," she said. "All of us. Fast." And Banks, who could talk anybody into anything, and knew exactly what it cost him not to, put his hands in his pockets and looked up at that enormous, patient, grinning face one more time, and said: "Yeah." They walked back to the treeline before the light went. Nobody talked about it again, and everybody thought about it for the rest of the night.

docs.title: The Hollow
docs.text:
A hunting cabin at the end of a washed-out logging road, tucked into a fold of the ridge above Soddy-Daisy — thick log walls, a single door, shuttered windows, and a wood stove that doesn't announce itself with electric light. The forest is the real wall here: the road in is so overgrown and washed out that vehicles can't make the last half-mile, so anything coming for you comes on foot, and you hear it first. Nine people live inside a cabin built for deer season.

Capacity 1 · Defense 2 — the survivors' haven.

docs.title: Before
docs.text: It was the Banks family cabin — Johnathan Banks' father's place, or his grandfather's. Built for deer season, not for the end of the world. Banks was a rich, snarky punk who barely used it, and it is the only thing he owned that turned out to matter.

docs.title: Now
docs.text:
Nine people: the four survivors and the five who were already here — Birdie Coyle, Sister Ruth Okafor, Tucker Vance, Marcus Webb, and Dale Pruitt. Capacity is rated for far fewer. People sleep on floors and outside.

They chose the sector deliberately: near Soddy-Daisy, with river access and natural resources close at hand, but not sitting on top of Chattanooga and whatever is still living in it. There are islands out in the water, noted as an escape route nobody has needed yet.

docs.title: What It Can't Do
docs.text:
• One way in, one way out. The logging road is easy to block or booby-trap — and just as easy for somebody else to block first. There is no good way to run.
  • The root cellar's nearly bare. Whoever lived here before cleaned it out. Hunting and foraging aren't optional; they're survival.
  • Woodsmoke gives you away. The stove is the only thing keeping nine people warm through a mountain winter, and its smoke can be seen and smelled from the valley below.
  • The well runs low in dry months. Fresh water isn't guaranteed once the summer heat sets in.

And the local threat undoes the one advantage the terrain was supposed to give them: the herds in these mountains climb. A cabin high on a ridge at the end of an impassable road is only safe from things that need a road.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — chosen as the haven over the Last Stop and the Ark, and established as Banks' family cabin.

docs.title: The Last Stop
docs.text:
An unfinished travel plaza off the old mountain highway — fifty fuel pumps under an unlit canopy, a gift shop the size of a barn, and a fifteen-foot fiberglass beaver still waving at an interstate nobody drives anymore. It never got its grand opening. The dry-storage shelves are still stocked with jerky and candy, the walk-in coolers went warm years ago, and the whole plaza can be seen from miles off in every direction. There is enough floor space here to house a small army, which is roughly what it would take to hold it.

Capacity 2 · Defense 1 — considered as a haven and passed over.

docs.title: Why They Didn't Take It
docs.text: The survivors wanted it badly. Johnathan Banks in particular had designs on being King Buc-ee and spreading the gospel of the beaver. The group talked themselves out of it in about a minute: they would die horrible, horrible, painful deaths, very quickly.

docs.title: Issues
docs.text:
• Too big to lock down. Between the fuel islands, the loading dock, and the shattered storefront windows, there are more ways in than anyone can watch.
  • Visible for miles. The mascot and the sheer size of the plaza make it an obvious landmark — for travelers, raiders, and herds alike.
  • Bone-dry tanks. The underground fuel was drained by looters years ago, which doesn't stop desperate people from turning up hoping to siphon something.
  • The propane cage out back is still full. One stray round or grease fire and the whole plaza goes up.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — offered as a haven option and rejected in favor of the Hollow. Floated afterward as a possible destination for one of Banks' letters of introduction.

docs.title: The Old Yeller
docs.text: A school bus sitting where it stopped on a mountain road, yellow paint gone chalky under five years of weather, windows fogged from the inside. Everyone in this stretch of Tennessee gives directions by it. The story goes that the driver had a heart attack behind the wheel and turned with a full load of children still aboard — and that some of them are still on it. People say the bus is haunted. People also say you should give it room, which is the part they actually mean.

docs.title: The Story
docs.text:
The driver had a heart attack. Then he turned. The bus was full of kids.

That's all anyone tells you, and they tell it the same way every time, which is usually a sign a story has been polished by a lot of retelling. Whether it happened is a separate question from whether people believe it. Everybody believes it.

Some say the bus is haunted. Nobody has volunteered to go and check.

docs.title: As A Landmark
docs.text: It is the fixed point in a region where the maps stopped being useful — the thing you navigate by, the thing you agree to meet at, the thing you tell a stranger to look for. Which means everyone in these mountains, friend or otherwise, knows exactly where it is.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — established during the Unsetting Questions as the region's landmark wreck, and named.

docs.title: Wanda "Birdie" Coyle
docs.text: Former Smoky Mountains Park Ranger · Resident of the Hollow · Anchor to Clara "CJ" James

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
"I know these mountains better than I know most people, and I'm at peace with that."

Sharp-eyed and steady under pressure, Birdie spent years reading these ridgelines long before the world fell apart, and she hasn't stopped since. She doesn't say much until she's decided you're worth the words — but once she has, she'll walk into the dark for you without blinking.

Of the nine people at the Hollow, she is the one whose knowledge the group is most likely to need and least likely to ask for. If anyone can tell them how a herd gets up a mountainside, it's the ranger.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Watchful, dry sense of humor, fiercely protective, more sentimental than she'd ever admit.

docs.title: Looking For
docs.text: Someone who keeps their word, and doesn't need everything spelled out twice.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: Survival. She reads terrain, weather, and animal sign the way other people read a room.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Clara "CJ" James — her Anchor. They bonded over a shared love of nature and growing things, a tie built at the Hollow rather than before it. Birdie keeps the mountains alive in her head; CJ is trying to grow something out of a root cellar that's nearly bare. It is the gentlest relationship in the group, and it belongs to its most dangerous member.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — introduced as one of the five already living at the Hollow; taken as CJ's Anchor over a shared love of growing things.

docs.title: Dale Pruitt
docs.text: Hill-Country Moonshiner · Resident of the Hollow · Anchor to Dr. Charles Greenbriar

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
"Come on by the still sometime. Bring your own cup."

Slow to trust, quick with a joke once he does. Dale's got a face that scares strangers off before he's said a word, and a heart that gives the lie to it about thirty seconds later. He knows this land, knows people, and knows exactly how to talk his way through a bad situation.

He is the reason Chuck Greenbriar is alive. Chuck came to Chattanooga for the aquarium, heard from locals about a moonshiner up in the hills, and went looking. He stayed at Dale's cabin until the two of them were driven out into the wilderness, and they walked together until they found the Hollow.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Loyal once you're in, proud of what he's built, folksy sense of humor, generous to a fault with people he likes.

docs.title: Looking For
docs.text: Someone who'll sit on the porch a while and not need the silence filled.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Dr. Charles Greenbriar — his Anchor, and the man he took in before any of this. Chuck's description of the bond is blunt: "Dale sees things when he's at the bottom of a bottle. He feeds my delusions." Whether Dale is humoring him, believes it too, or has simply never had a reason to argue is an open question.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — introduced; taken as Chuck Greenbriar's Anchor. Established as the pair's shared history before the Hollow.

docs.title: Marcus Webb
docs.text: Age 15 · Resident of the Hollow

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
"Everybody still treats me like a kid. I'd rather you just see what I can actually do."

Marcus doesn't remember much about before — this world is the only one he really knows. Quick, restless, and always looking for a way to prove himself useful, he's easy to underestimate and hates being underestimated.

He is the only child at the Hollow, and the only person there who has never known anything else. That makes him the one the others instinctively protect, and the one most likely to resent it.

It also puts him at the sharp end of the strangest thing anyone in these mountains has reported: that a walker was once seen to pause before attacking a child. Nobody knows what that means. Nobody wants to find out using Marcus.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Curious, a little too bold for his own good, fiercely protective of the few things he has left from before.

docs.title: Looking For
docs.text: A friend, an older-sibling type, or someone willing to take him seriously. Not looking for anything romantic — just someone who'll actually listen when he has something to say, and maybe teach him something worth knowing.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: No survivor took Marcus as an Anchor. He and Tucker Vance are the two residents of the Hollow with no PC tie — which, for a fifteen-year-old who wants to be taken seriously, is its own kind of answer.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — introduced as one of the five already at the Hollow, and as the group's only minor. Unclaimed as an Anchor.

docs.title: Sister Ruth Okafor
docs.text: Former Hospice Nurse · Resident of the Hollow · Anchor to Johnathan Banks

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
"I've sat with a lot of people at the end of something. I'd rather sit with you at the start of something good."

Calm in a way that can feel almost otherworldly, Ruth has a gift for making even the worst moments feel survivable. Her faith isn't loud, but it's steady, and so is she — the kind of presence that makes a room exhale.

She was not at the Hollow by accident. Johnathan Banks found her at the retirement home — one of the havens he carries a letter of introduction to — and talked her into walking away from it. His pitch, by his own account: "Just read these people their last rites and then come help us." She came.

Nobody has asked her how she feels about that. It is the single largest unpaid debt in the group.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Warm, unshakably patient, quietly stubborn, notices more than she lets on.

docs.title: Looking For
docs.text: Someone who could use a little looking after, and won't be too proud to admit it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Johnathan Banks — her Anchor, and the man who recruited her out of the retirement home. He is fully aware of what he did.
  • The retirement home — the people she left behind. They are, presumably, still there.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — introduced; taken as Johnathan Banks' Anchor. Her recruitment from the retirement home was established as the story behind that bond.

docs.title: The Watchman
docs.text: Voice on the wrong frequency · Location unknown

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Tune a little too far past where you meant to stop and you might find him: a man who calls himself the Watchman, after the graphic novel, which he took very seriously. He talks conspiracy — the chemicals in the water, what they really put in it, what it's turning people into. He is deep in the Kool-Aid and he is extremely confident.

The important thing about him is not what he says. It's that the broadcasts keep changing. It isn't a loop and it isn't a recording playing to an empty room. Every so often there's a new one, which means that somewhere out there, five years in, the Watchman is still alive and still transmitting.

Nobody knows where he broadcasts from. Nobody has met him. One day the broadcasts will stop, and everyone who has been listening will know exactly what that means.

docs.title: What He Claims
docs.text:
• It's the chemicals in the water. It's the fluoride. That's what's turning them.
  • Whatever else he's said, somebody out here has repeated it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: None established. He is a voice, not yet a person — though the survivors have noted that a man who never stops talking on an open frequency is a man who can be found.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — established during the Unsetting Questions as the piece of radio chatter everyone in this region still talks about.

docs.title: Tucker Vance
docs.text: Auto Mechanic, Chattanooga · Resident of the Hollow

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
"I can fix pretty much anything. Might take me a minute to trust you, though."

Big hands, bigger heart, terrible at small talk. Tucker's happiest elbow-deep in an engine, muttering to himself, and surprisingly easy to win over once you show him you respect the work. Loyal to the end, once you're in.

At a haven half a mile past where any vehicle can reach, a mechanic is either useless or the most important person there, depending entirely on what comes up the logging road next.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Hardworking, gentle underneath the gruff exterior, deeply loyal, a worrier at heart.

docs.title: Looking For
docs.text: Someone patient enough to let him warm up in his own time — and who won't rush a good repair job.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: No survivor anchored to Tucker. He was briefly considered — Johnathan Banks weighed him before settling on Sister Ruth — and then passed over. He and Marcus Webb are the two residents of the Hollow with no PC tie.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — introduced as one of the five already at the Hollow. Considered as an Anchor and left unclaimed.

docs.title: Ashley Fairfax
docs.text: Player: Graycen · Archetype: Nobody · Issue: Doesn't care if she lives · Drive: "Keeps going anyway"

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Ash was a college dropout and a burnout — smoked weed, didn't do much else, and wasn't looking forward to the rat race she'd walked away from. She misses it now. That's the joke of her, and it isn't funny to her.

She was delivering a pizza when it happened. Caught out in a herd mid-delivery, she booked it into the woods and kept going, and she has been going ever since. She stumbled onto the cabin at the end of the logging road the way she stumbles onto most things. Of the four survivors at the Hollow, she is the one everybody knows least.

She does not particularly care whether she lives. She has not stopped moving. Both of those are true at once, and the second one is the only reason she's here.

docs.title: In Character
docs.text:
"Wasn't looking forward to the rat race. Miss it now."

Issue — she doesn't really care if she lives.

Drive — "Keeps going anyway." Her drive loops straight back into her issue, which is the point.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
• Talent: Wallflower. She doesn't take a single NPC as her Anchor — the whole group is her anchor. Her stated reason: "So I don't get as sad if one of them dies." It also means that if they all die, she has nothing left to steady her.
  • Gear: a machete, a frying pan, and a fishing rod. "We're packing light."

docs.title: Anchor
docs.text: The whole group, by way of the Wallflower talent — no single NPC. A hedge against grief that is also a bet she can't win twice.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Johnathan Banks — she showed up at his cabin and he let her stay. That's the whole of it so far.
  • Dr. Charles Greenbriar — she may have called the cops on him back in Chattanooga, before everything. Neither of them has fully committed to that story.
  • Clara "CJ" James — no history before the Hollow.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — created; established as the group's outsider, joining by accident rather than by any tie. Took the Wallflower talent, making the survivors themselves her Anchor.

docs.title: Dr. Charles Greenbriar
docs.text: Player: Conner · Archetype: Scientist · Drive: "I'm not crazy"

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
He introduces himself as Dr. Charles Greenbriar. He goes by Chuck. Whether the doctorate is real is, in his own group's assessment, dubious.

What is not in dispute is that he trained as a biologist, and that what he actually wanted to do with it was cryptozoology. He never got the chance — and then the dead started walking, which he takes as vindication. He is convinced the walkers connect to the thing he spent his career being laughed at for. There is something about them. He is going to prove it.

His working theory, offered without hedging, is that the outbreak began when Bigfoot caught COVID.

He came to Chattanooga for the aquarium. He met locals who told him about a moonshiner up in the hills, went looking for him, and stayed at Dale Pruitt's cabin until the two of them were forced out into the wilderness. They walked until they found somebody else's cabin, and that is how the Hollow got two more mouths.

docs.title: In Character
docs.text:
"I'm not crazy."

"They are real. It's a hundred percent right."

"When Bigfoot got COVID — that's what happened."

Drive — "I'm not crazy." He made it up rather than take one off the list.

Flaw — morally flexible, and running on a delusion nobody at the Hollow has the heart to puncture.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
• Gear: a firearm, a sledgehammer, and a portable gas stove with a lighter. The image the table settled on is a man waving a sledgehammer and a gun, insisting he is not crazy.
  • No medicine. The group noticed. The group is not thrilled.

docs.title: Anchor
docs.text: Dale Pruitt — the moonshiner who took him in before any of this. Chuck's read on the relationship is unusually honest: "Dale sees things when he's at the bottom of a bottle. He feeds my delusions." It is a genuine bond and a closed loop at the same time, and everyone else can see the second part.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Johnathan Banks — arrived on Banks' doorstep as a stranger out of the woods and was allowed to stay.
  • Ashley Fairfax — she may have called the cops on him in Chattanooga, before.
  • Clara "CJ" James — the person he'd most like standing between him and a herd.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — created; arrived at the Hollow with Dale Pruitt after being driven out of Dale's cabin. Took Dale as his Anchor. Established the Bigfoot theory of the outbreak, which nobody has agreed to and nobody has contradicted.

docs.title: Clara James
docs.text: Player: Cobie · Archetype: Homemaker · Issue: Bloodthirsty · Drive: Take down as many as possible

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
CJ was a homemaker in a good neighborhood, the kind with pilates on the calendar and a martial-arts class squeezed in between school runs and soccer practice. She has no family now. What she has instead is a number she is trying to run up.

She is the most dangerous person at the Hollow and everyone there knows it. When the group weighed taking the indefensible Buc-ee's plaza, the argument against it was that they would all die — and the argument for it was, essentially, we've got CJ. Somebody said they weren't relying entirely on CJ. Nobody believed them.

She was Johnathan Banks' neighbor before the outbreak — another wealthy household on the same street. He took her with him when it fell apart. It is not clear which of them got the better end of that.

docs.title: In Character
docs.text:
"Quick with that rolling pin. Or a knife."

Issue — Bloodthirsty.

Drive — take down as many as possible. She wants revenge for her family, and the arithmetic of it is the closest thing she has to a plan.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
• Favorite attribute: Agility, taken to 5 — the highest number anyone at the Hollow put anywhere.
  • Built for close combat. The table's image of her is a soccer mom with the training actually behind it.
  • Gear: among the group's better hauls — a car, bone arrows, and a bag of medicinal herbs.

docs.title: Anchor
docs.text:
Birdie Coyle — the former park ranger. They bonded over a shared love of nature and growing things, which is the softest fact established about CJ all session and sits at an odd angle to everything else about her. They didn't know each other before; the bond was built at the Hollow.

It is worth noting what she chose. The most lethal person at the haven anchored herself not to a fighter but to the woman who knows how to make things live.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Johnathan Banks — her neighbor from before, and the man who got her out. The oldest tie in the group.
  • Dr. Charles Greenbriar — he'd like to hide behind her, and says so.
  • Birdie Coyle — her Anchor, and her one established interest outside of killing.
  • Ashley Fairfax — no history before the Hollow.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — created; established as the group's protector and its only real combatant. Took Birdie Coyle as her Anchor over a shared love of growing things. Her relationship with Banks — neighbors before, survivors after — is the oldest bond among the four.

docs.title: Johnathan Banks
docs.text: Player: Ian · Archetype: Broker (homebrew) · Drive: "I just gotta ring the bell"

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Wall Street didn't end when the world did — not for Johnathan Banks. He still talks in positions and upside, still reads a room like a spread, and still believes, somewhere under all of it, that the market is coming back and he will be standing there when the bell rings. He goes by JB, or Johnny B. Someone floated "Banksy" once; he didn't take to it. "I'm not into that art stuff. The only art I see is stocks going up and down."

Before the outbreak he ran insider trades for mobsters. He rather hopes they're all dead. They probably aren't.

The cabin the survivors now live in is his — the Banks family place, his father's or his grandfather's, at the end of a logging road nobody maintained even when there was somebody to maintain it. He was a rich, snarky punk with a hunting cabin he barely used, and he has spent the five years since taking in stragglers against what he insists is his better judgment. He is not warm about it. He keeps doing it anyway.

He carries no weapon. He carries letters of introduction to three other havens, which he considers the better armament.

docs.title: In Character
docs.text:
"I like the hockey stick. Up and to the right."

"You're necessary for me to live."

"Y'all are gonna hate me, but you'll need me."

Drive — get back to Wall Street. "I just gotta ring the bell."

Flaw — morally flexible, and cheerfully aware of it. He intends to be the kind of man the group wants to kill and can't afford to.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
• Key skill: Manipulation. Empathy is his best attribute, and he spent his points on talking people into things.
  • Talent: Silver Tongue.
  • Gear: sorted small-value trade goods; a set of scales to weigh them; and letters of introduction to three other havens. He rolled the scales twice — "in case one of them's off, I like to check my work."
  • No weapon at all.

docs.title: Anchor
docs.text: Sister Ruth Okafor — the hospice nurse. He met her at the retirement home, one of the havens he holds a letter for, and talked her into leaving with him: "Just read these people their last rites and then come help us." He recruited her to the Hollow. He is entirely clear-eyed that this was an awful thing to do and did it anyway.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Clara "CJ" James — his neighbor from before, another wealthy household on the same street. When it fell apart he took her with him. She is the reason the cabin is still standing.
  • Dr. Charles Greenbriar — arrived at the Hollow as a stranger, on foot, out of the woods, with Dale Pruitt in tow.
  • Ashley Fairfax — pure happenstance. She turned up. He let her stay.

docs.title: Session History
docs.text: • Nine in the Hollow — established as the owner of the Hollow and the reluctant reason anyone else is living in it. Took Sister Ruth as his Anchor. Confirmed the retirement home as one of his three letters of introduction; the other two are still open.
